The Election of 1968. Richard Nixon's comeback victory over Vice President Hubert Humphrey ended a generation of Democratic dominance and marked a decisive turn to the right. Nixon won forty-three point four percent of the popular vote and three hundred one electoral votes, carrying the South and suburbs while Humphrey, hamstrung by Johnson's unpopular war in Vietnam, managed only forty-two point seven percent.

Richard Nixon campaigned as the law and order candidate, promising to end the Vietnam War through peace with honor while cracking down on urban crime and protests. Hubert Humphrey, the sitting vice president, was crippled by his association with Lyndon Johnson's Vietnam escalation; he could not break free without repudiating his president. George Wallace, the Alabama governor and segregationist, captured nearly fourteen percent of the popular vote and forty-six electoral votes—the strongest third-party showing since nineteen twelve—running against pointy-headed intellectuals and civil rights expansion.

The Tet Offensive in January nineteen sixty-eight turned American public opinion decisively against the war; by spring, Johnson withdrew from the race. The assassinations of Martin Luther King Junior in April and Robert Kennedy in June further destabilized the country and energized backlash politics. Urban riots, antiwar protests, and student unrest created a sense of social crisis that favored law-and-order messages.

Nixon's Southern Strategy explicitly courted white southern Democrats alienated by civil rights; the South began its shift toward the GOP. Humphrey's narrow loss of zero point seven percent nationally masked a deeper Democratic fracture: the working-class and ethnic voters who had built the New Deal Coalition were shifting toward Nixon and Wallace. Nixon's presidency brought détente with the Soviet Union and Watergate—the scandal that would terminate his presidency.
